title: Parents as they are
hook: honor thy father and thy mother (Exodus 20:12), with honest boundaries

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Emerson: the only way to have a friend is to be one. Your line was tend it.

A grown woman pulls into her parents' driveway and sits in the car for a minute before going in. Engine off. Hands on the wheel. Inside is the man who taught her to ride a bike, and who still knows exactly which comment will make her feel twelve years old. She loves him. She's also bracing. Both are true at once, and neither cancels the other. Ancient law codes, sages and scriptures all speak about parents: what honoring them asks, and what it doesn't.
screen: `SITTING IN THE CAR FOR A MINUTE.` → `LOVING AND BRACING AT ONCE.` → `WHAT HONOR ASKS, AND DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: First, the commandment. Among the Ten Commandments in Exodus: "Honour thy father and thy mother." It doesn't say love them warmly at every moment, or agree with them, or pretend they were perfect. It says honor. Second, honor is actions. The rabbis of the Talmud asked what honoring a parent looks like, and their answers are concrete: providing food and drink, clothing, helping them come and go. Reverence, they said, means things like not standing or sitting in a parent's place and not contradicting their words. Honor is something you do, whatever you happen to feel that afternoon. Third, Confucius on support. In the Analects, Confucius notes that in his day filial duty is taken to mean simply feeding your parents. But dogs and horses get fed too, he says. Without respect, what's the difference? Elsewhere he says a child may disagree with a parent, but gently. Even in a tradition that places parents very high, honest disagreement has a place. Fourth, honor with boundaries. Leviticus pairs two commands in one breath: "Ye shall fear every man his mother, and his father, and keep my sabbaths." The rabbis read that pairing as a limit: if a parent tells a child to break the sabbath, the child doesn't obey, because parent and child both answer to God. Honor has edges. For people whose parents caused real harm, some teachers say honor can mean decency kept at a safe distance. Parents as they are: not as we wish they were, and not more than they are either.
screen: `HONOR YOUR FATHER AND MOTHER.` · `HONOR IS ACTIONS.` · `CONFUCIUS: FEEDING ISN'T ENOUGH.` · `HONOR WITH BOUNDARIES.` · then, large: `AS THEY ARE.`

segments.voice: Let a parent, a grandparent or an elder who raised you come to mind; if they've died, remembering is a form of honor too. See them as they are or were, their age, their tiredness, the history they carried, and let one thing they gave you sit beside one boundary you need with them, without the two arguing. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name.
Kabed. The Hebrew verb behind honor thy father and thy mother, shown in concrete acts of care, not just feeling. Today's word.
Your line: as they are. Honor can be a full plate, a gentle word, or decency at a safe distance. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews and Christians count honoring parents among the Ten Commandments, and Jewish law spells it out in concrete acts of care; in Confucian tradition filial respect is central, and families honor elders through visits, care and remembrance.

chat.says: Does honoring my parents mean I have to do whatever they say?
options: No. Honor means acts of care and respect, and the rabbis set limits on obeying.
Yes. The commandment means total obedience, even when they ask for something wrong.
No. Honor only means feeling grateful; you don't owe them any actions at all.
chat.meaning: The rabbis read Leviticus 19:3 as a limit: parent and child both answer to God. Honor, for them, is concrete care like food, clothing and help.
